name: Matthew
author: Christians have traditionally credited this gospel to Matthew, also called Levi, a tax collector who left his booth to become one of Jesus' twelve apostles. Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling powers, often took extra for themselves, and were widely despised by fellow Jews. Many modern scholars think the book was written by an unnamed Jewish Christian teacher who drew on Mark's gospel and a collection of Jesus' sayings, with Matthew's name attached early on. Either way, the writer knew the Jewish Scriptures and customs closely.
audience: It was written mainly for Jewish followers of Jesus, perhaps in Syria around the city of Antioch or in Galilee, along with non-Jews joining their churches. They were working out how faith in Jesus fitted with their Jewish heritage, often amid painful arguments with local synagogue leaders.
era: Jesus lived under Roman rule, with local kings from Herod's family and Roman governors such as Pontius Pilate in charge. The gospel was most likely written around AD 70–90, though some date it to the 60s. In AD 66 the Jews revolted against Rome, and in AD 70 Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Afterwards, Jewish life regrouped largely around the synagogue and the teaching of the Pharisees.

notes.2:1: Herod the Great, Rome's appointed king of Judea, died around 4 BC. The magi were likely learned star-watchers from the east, perhaps Persia or Babylon.
notes.2:13: Egypt, a Roman province outside Herod's kingdom, had large Jewish communities, especially in the city of Alexandria. Later in this passage, after Herod died, his son Archelaus ruled Judea so harshly that Rome removed him in AD 6; Galilee, where Nazareth lay, went to another son, Herod Antipas.
notes.3:1: John baptised in the Jordan River near the Judean desert, probably around AD 28. Pharisees were strict keepers of Jewish law; Sadducees were the wealthy priestly party.
notes.4:12: Capernaum was a busy fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, in the territory of Herod Antipas, who had arrested John.
notes.4:23: This passage moves from Jesus travelling Galilee's towns, teaching in their synagogues (local meeting houses where Jews gathered to pray and hear the Scriptures read), to the start of his teaching on a hillside. That hillside is traditionally placed above the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum.
notes.5:38: Under Roman rule, soldiers could force civilians to carry their gear for a distance.
notes.8:5: A centurion was an army officer over about a hundred men, probably a non-Jew serving Herod Antipas or Rome at Capernaum.
notes.8:28: The region of the Gadarenes lay on the southeast side of the Sea of Galilee, a largely non-Jewish area, which is why pigs were kept there.
notes.9:9: This is the call of the man tradition names as the gospel's author, sitting at a toll booth, probably in Capernaum.
notes.11:20: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were Jewish towns near the north end of the lake; Tyre and Sidon were wealthy non-Jewish ports on the Mediterranean coast.
notes.14:1: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee for Rome. The Jewish historian Josephus says John was held at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.
notes.15:21: Tyre and Sidon were non-Jewish coastal cities in what is now Lebanon, northwest of Galilee.
notes.16:13: Caesarea Philippi lay near the foot of Mount Hermon, by a spring with a shrine to the Greek god Pan; Herod's son Philip renamed it honouring Caesar.
notes.17:1: The mountain is not named; it is traditionally identified as Mount Tabor in Galilee, though some suggest Mount Hermon.
notes.17:22: Later in this passage, collectors ask about the temple tax, a yearly payment of two drachmas, about two days' wages, expected of Jewish men to support the Jerusalem temple.
notes.19:1: Jewish teachers of the day were divided on divorce: one school allowed it for many reasons, another, stricter school mainly for unfaithfulness.
notes.20:29: Jericho was the last town on the pilgrim road before the steep climb of about fifteen miles up to Jerusalem.
notes.21:1: Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims arriving for Passover. Bethphage and the Mount of Olives lay just east of the city.
notes.21:12: In the temple's outer court, traders sold animals for sacrifice and money changers swapped pilgrims' coins for the special currency used for temple payments.
notes.22:15: The Herodians supported Herod's family. The tax in question was paid to Rome in silver coins bearing the emperor's image, and was deeply resented.
notes.22:23: The Sadducees, the priestly upper class, gave the five books of Moses chief authority (some think they accepted only these) and did not believe in resurrection.
notes.24:1: Herod the Great had rebuilt and greatly enlarged the temple; work was still continuing in Jesus' day. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.
notes.26:6: Bethany was a village about two miles east of Jerusalem, on the far side of the Mount of Olives.
notes.26:17: Passover was the yearly meal remembering Israel's escape from Egypt, eaten in Jerusalem with lamb, unleavened bread and wine.
notes.26:36: Gethsemane, meaning "oil press", was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, just across the Kidron Valley from the city walls.
notes.26:57: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36. The council, called the Sanhedrin, was the Jewish ruling body in Jerusalem under Rome.
notes.27:11: Pontius Pilate was Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, in Jerusalem for Passover to keep order; Rome generally kept the power of execution in its own hands.
notes.27:32: Crucifixion took place outside the city walls, probably around AD 30 or 33. Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in present-day Libya.
notes.27:57: Arimathea was a Judean town. Wealthy families had tombs cut into rock, sealed with a large stone rolled across the entrance.

flags.problem: The note opens with "This is the call…", so it reads as if it covers only verse 9. The passage runs to verse 13 and includes the meal that follows, so a reader on verses 10–13 may be confused.
flags.suggestion: Word it for the whole passage, e.g. "This passage opens with the call of the man tradition names as the gospel's author, sitting at a toll booth, probably in Capernaum."
